sources.title: The Nimzowitsch Defense: A How to Play Guide (as White & Black)
Search snippet: Nimzowitsch Defense overview (Advance Variation, Bogoljubov 3.Nc3, Kasparov/Keene quote)

overview: Black develops a knight on move one and invites White to build a centre, planning to undermine it with timely pieces and pawn breaks (...d5, ...e5 or ...e6). The most common reply to 2.d4 is 2...d5 with 3.exd5 Qxd5 (Scandinavian-type), 3.e5 Bf5 (French-Advance-like with a freed bishop) or the 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.d5 Ne5 line, which is French-like in structure. Alternatively Black plays 2...e5 (Kennedy Variation), which can transpose to the Scotch, or 2...e6/2...g6 (Franco-Hiva, Pirc connection) with flexible set-ups. Kasparov and Keene wrote it has never been fully accepted as dependable, but sources agree it is far from refuted; players choose it to escape preparation and play non-standard but often French/Scandinavian-like middlegames. Roughly 2% of games per Chessable.

white_ideas.idea: Seize the centre with 2.d4 and build a pawn centre and space advantage
Meet 2.d4 d5 with 3.e5 Bf5 4.c3, a long pawn chain and dark-square control, or 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.d5 Ne5 chasing the knight
Play 2.Nf3, which forces Black into main-line theory (2...e5) or leaves Black with inferior chances if he resists

black_ideas.idea: Delay committing and watch what White does; transpose into Scandinavian-like or French-like positions
Hypermodern: invite the centre, then block or restrain it and strike with ...d5, ...e5, or ...e6
Use 3...Bf5 against the Advance to get the light-squared bishop out before ...e6
Kennedy Variation 2.d4 e5: solid approach favoured by Tony Miles, which may transpose to the Scotch

typical_structures.structure: French-Advance-like chain (e5/d4/c3 vs ...e6/...d5) with Black's bishop outside the chain after ...Bf5
Scandinavian-type positions after 3.exd5 Qxd5 with White ahead in development
Open Scotch-like centre after 2...e5 and exchanges

character.notes: Sources describe a non-committal, 'test' type of opening with limited theory; main-line positions are French/Scandinavian-like and relatively quiet. Provocative flank-style counterplay is the idea, not sharp forced play. Sideline gambits (Colorado Gambit 2.Nf3 f5, Franco-Hiva) are sharp.

gambit.notes: No gambit in the root. Sidelines: Colorado Gambit (2.Nf3 f5, called sharp but dubious) and Franco-Hiva Gambit in the subtree. The Bogoljubov 3.Nc3 dxe4 line functions like a gambit but Black generally keeps a French-like structure.

soundness.notes: Kasparov and Keene: 'has never been fully accepted as a dependable opening'. Chessable: 'far from refuted' yet speculative, and it is probably better for Black to transpose earlier into something more main line. Wikipedia: sound for those seeking foreign territory. So respectable but a slight concession against best play.

structure.notes: Depends on branch: French-Advance-like closed chain (3.e5), Scandinavian-like semi-open (3.exd5 Qxd5), or open Scotch (2...e5). Most main-line play is partly open to closed.

approach.notes: Not a universal system; Black's reply depends on White's move 2. It is a rare opening (about 2% of games per Chessable) chosen to escape preparation. Historically played by Nimzowitsch and Bogoljubov, Hort, Miles and others, so it has had strong players, but it is not a mainstream choice. Chessable calls it an offbeat non-theoretical opening and more of a test than a self-sufficient system.

level.notes: Chessable: moderate-to-challenging for club players because limited theory plus frequent transpositions means the player must know several structures. Little move memorisation but White can steer into several different set-ups.

plan_phrases: transposition to Scandinavian or French structures

sublines_that_differ.name: Scandinavian Variation / 3.e5 Advance
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. e4 Nc6 2. d4 d5 3. e5 Bf5
sublines_that_differ.how: French-Advance-like chain; Black gets the bishop outside before ...e6.

sublines_that_differ.name: Bogoljubov Variation
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. e4 Nc6 2. d4 d5 3. Nc3 dxe4 4. d5 Ne5
sublines_that_differ.how: Gambit-like, French-style positions with a knight on e5.

sublines_that_differ.name: Colorado / Lean Gambit
sublines_that_differ.how: Aggressive Black gambit; sharp but dubious.

sublines_that_differ.name: Franco-Hiva Gambit
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. e4 Nc6 2. d4 e6 3. Nf3 f5 4. exf5 Nf6
sublines_that_differ.how: Rare Black gambit in the subtree.

description.claim: Black develops a knight instead of a pawn to challenge White's central control immediately
description.note: 1...Nc6 is a hypermodern idea: invite the centre then challenge it.

description.claim: It is a hypermodern opening where Black aims to undermine White's centre from the flanks
description.note: Wikipedia characterises it as hypermodern. 'From the flanks' is loose: Black's main counterplay comes from central breaks (...d5, ...e5) and piece pressure, not flank play.

description.claim: It leads to complex and non-standard positions with less theory
description.note: Limited theory and transpositions per Chessable.

description.claim: The opening's character is one of patient counter-attack
description.note: Tone; sources describe a non-committal first move waiting to see White's intentions.

common_plans.claim: Black: challenge White's centre, typically with an early ...d5
Black: fianchetto the king's bishop (...g6, ...Bg7) to pressure d4
common_plans.note: 2.d4 g6 is a Pirc connection in the subtree, but it is a minority line, not the main plan.

common_plans.claim: White: seize the centre with 2.d4 and develop quickly to exploit space
White: restrain Black's ...d5 pawn break and consolidate before attacking
common_plans.note: In the main lines White does not try to prevent ...d5; 3.e5 and 3.Nc3 are used after Black plays it. Chessable's best reply is 2.Nf3 with transposition to normal theory instead. Own judgement on 'wrong'; partially misleading rather than incorrect chess.
